summary_sentence: XYZ and quadkeys are two ways to address map tiles. The coordinate workspace here does not calculate either; dedicated tile tools are linked below.

Tile-keyed imagery and statistics may be joined using a validated XYZ-to-quadkey conversion.

032010110132021 decodes digit by digit from the top of the pyramid: each digit (0–3) picks a quadrant — NW, NE, SW, SE in the quadkey convention — and the string's length IS the zoom (15 digits, zoom 15).
Drop the last digit and you hold the parent tile at zoom 14; drop four, the zoom-11 ancestor. Quadkeys make tile genealogy a string operation — the property databases love.

popular_table.title: Two dialects, one grid
popular_table.intro: XYZ and quadkey describe the same pyramid.
popular_table.note: A quadkey encodes tile x and y bits as base-4 digits. The coordinate workspace on this page does not calculate tile addresses.

faq: A tile's address written as one string: each digit narrows to a quadrant, zoom equals length. Bing Maps popularised it; tile-keyed databases adopted it.
Each level has four children. Two bits per level — one from x, one from y — make one base-4 digit.
Yes — the Web Mercator slippy pyramid. Quadkey and XYZ are two notations for identical tiles (modulo the TMS y-flip some stacks apply).
Use the zoom associated with your data. This workspace does not calculate tile addresses; use a dedicated tile calculator.
A region may cover multiple tiles. This workspace does not calculate the tiles or quadkeys for it.
A quadkey names a whole tile, not a point — at zoom 15 in New York, a ~926 m square. Finer zooms name smaller squares.
Entirely — '032...' and '32...' are different tiles at different zooms. Never store quadkeys as numbers; the zeros are load-bearing.
